examples.text: A magnetic field model draws curved lines around a magnet to show the invisible force that pulls or pushes other magnets!
Models can represent objects that are too big to see all at once, like the whole Earth.
A model is not an exact copy! It leaves out extra details so scientists can focus on the most important parts.
Models may be physical objects, drawings, or mathematical equations, and they are not perfect copies.
Did you know everything around us is made of countless atoms?

Why does a snowflake have six sides?

Because of how its water molecules line up!
When you dissolve salt in water, you are making a mixture, not a pure substance!
A pure substance is made of just one kind of particle! But a mixture physically combines two or more different substances together.
The hotter an object gets, the faster its tiny particles zoom and move around inside it!
When cooled, particles move more slowly and pack closer together, so the object contracts!
During expansion, the particles themselves don't get bigger—only the space between them increases!
Railway tracks have small gaps between rails so they have room to expand when hot and do not buckle!
Water molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds! These are special attractions between the H of one molecule and the O of another, giving water high surface tension.

Why do substances become solid?

The state of a substance depends on how strongly its particles attract each other. The stronger the attraction, the more likely it is a solid!
When you heat saltwater, water molecules gain energy to escape as water vapor, leaving the solid salt behind!
Ice left outside on a hot sunny day in Manila melts into liquid water because heat increases molecular motion!
When making rock candy, dissolved sugar molecules slowly arrange themselves into a structured solid lattice during the crystallization stage!

How do particles act in a solid?

In a solid like rock, tiny particles are packed close together. They only vibrate in place and do not move away from each other!

Draw three particle diagrams using equal-sized dots. Solid: closely spaced dots in fixed positions with small vibration arrows. Liquid: close dots in an irregular arrangement, moving past one another. Gas: widely spaced dots with arrows in different directions. The dots represent particles, not their actual size or color.
Cooling a liquid can change it back to a solid, because the particles slow down and lock into fixed positions again.

Draw three particle diagrams using equal-sized dots. Solid: closely spaced dots in fixed positions with small vibration arrows. Liquid: close dots in an irregular arrangement, moving past one another. Gas: widely spaced dots with arrows in different directions. The dots represent particles, not their actual size or color.
Applying pressure moves gas molecules closer together, decreasing the volume they occupy.

Liquid: close dots in an irregular arrangement, moving past one another. Gas: widely spaced dots with arrows in different directions. The dots represent particles, not their actual size or color.
In the Kelvin scale, water boils at about 373 Kelvin (373 K)!
Liquid water boils at 100°C, but liquid nitrogen boils at a much colder -196°C!
Putting water in a freezer removes heat, making molecules slow down and lock into solid ice!

During melting, energy lets particles leave fixed positions and move past one another. During evaporation, particles escape the liquid into widely spaced gas. Condensation and freezing release energy as particles form a liquid or solid arrangement. Adding heat during a change of state need not raise temperature; energy can change the arrangement instead.

Condensation and freezing release energy as particles form a liquid or solid arrangement. Adding heat during a change of state need not raise temperature; energy can change the arrangement instead.
During melting and evaporation, particle arrangement changes from tightly packed to loosely arranged to far apart as heat is added.
Write your aim as a question! Name the exact thing you will change and the thing you will measure.

How do you choose your materials and steps?

Your aim guides you! What you want to find out decides what you measure and how.

How do you choose your materials and steps?

Your aim guides you! What you want to find out decides what you measure and how.
Show your teacher the problem and materials list before mixing! This fixes any unsafe or untestable plans right away.
Writing a procedure? Use action words like 'measure', 'pour', and 'mix' so your steps are super clear!
A good experiment has a clear procedure, the step-by-step instructions you follow to test your hypothesis safely.
For repeated trials, give each trial its own row in the data table. Label each column with the measurement and its unit!
In the conclusion, compare your actual results with your aim! Say plainly what the data show, even if it is not what you wanted.
In the conclusion, compare your actual results with your aim! Say plainly what the data show, even if it is not what you wanted.

How do scientists solve mysteries?

They ask a question, make a hypothesis, test it with an experiment, and form a conclusion from the results!
Even though it's a volcano, Taal Volcano is only about 311 meters tall!
The kelvin (K) is the official SI base unit used to measure temperature!

To compare leaf lengths, line up the ruler’s zero mark with each leaf’s base. Read straight above the scale. Record each leaf in a separate table row, with a column headed Length (cm). Keep the same unit and record only the precision the ruler supports. Units make results interpretable; they do not by themselves guarantee accuracy.
Units of measure must always be included when reporting a measurement to ensure the data is accurate and clear.
For repeated trials, give each trial its own row in the data table. Label each column with the measurement and its unit!
A seismograph is an instrument that measures and records ground shaking during an earthquake. It is used by PHIVOLCS here in the Philippines!
A solution is a special mixture where the solute is spread evenly throughout the whole solvent!
When something dissolves, the substance dissolving is the solute, and the liquid dissolving it is the solvent!
A solution is a special mixture where the solute is spread evenly throughout the whole solvent!
Water is the "universal solvent" because more substances dissolve in it than in any other liquid!
One liter of seawater from Manila Bay holds about 33 grams of dissolved salts, mostly sodium chloride!
At room temperature, 100 mL of water can dissolve a maximum of 36 grams of table salt. That's the limit!

A class adds 5 g of sugar to 100 mL of water. The amount per volume of solvent is 5 g ÷ 100 mL = 0.05 g per mL of water. Do not call this 5% mass/volume of solution unless the final solution volume is 100 mL. Solvent volume before mixing and final solution volume are different quantities.

If you dissolve 90 mL of hydrogen peroxide to make 3000 mL of solution, what is the concentration?

It is 3%, because 90 divided by 3000 is 0.03, and 0.03 times 100 is 3!
At room temperature, 100 mL of water can dissolve a maximum of 36 grams of table salt. That's the limit!

How much sugar can water dissolve?

At 20°C, 100 milliliters of water can dissolve up to 200 grams of sugar!

Can warm water hold more salt than cold water?

Yes! Warm water dissolves a larger total amount of salt. Heat up saturated water, and it can take in even more!

Why does sugar disappear so fast in hot calamansi juice?

Sugar dissolves completely to form a clear solution because higher temperatures increase the sugar's solubility!
A glass of water can only hold so much sugar! Past that limit, extra sugar just won't dissolve.
There is a limit to how much solute can dissolve! When it is full, it is called saturated, and extra solute will not dissolve.

Does water dissolve the same amount of every substance?

No! In the same amount of water, much more sugar dissolves than salt because water dissolves different amounts of each substance.

With a teacher, compare how much sugar dissolves in equal volumes of water at two measured temperatures. Add weighed portions, stir and wait long enough; record the amount dissolved when extra sugar remains. Keep other conditions the same. This tests solubility, the maximum amount at that temperature, not just how fast a spoonful disappears.
Vinegar is acidic! It has a pH of about 3.
Orange juice is acidic! Its pH is about 3 to 4.
Household ammonia is a base! It has a pH of about 11.
Baking soda is basic (alkaline)! It has a pH of about 9.
Salted eggs are made by coating eggs in salty clay, or soaking them in salt water for several weeks.
Baking soda is actually sodium bicarbonate, which is a very special kind of chemical salt for baking!

What happens to red litmus paper in a base?

It turns blue in a base!
Did you know? BLUE litmus paper turns RED when it is dipped in an acid!

Use only teacher-approved samples: vinegar turns blue litmus red; a basic soap solution turns red litmus blue. A neutral table-salt solution changes neither. Litmus indicates acidic or basic behavior; it cannot prove that a solution contains salt. Some other salts form acidic or basic solutions. Never taste laboratory samples.

Why clean a thermometer?

We must clean a thermometer before and after use so it doesn't spread germs!

Why do some indicators need to be stored in dark places?

Strong light and air can make an indicator's color fade or spoil over time. An old or spoiled indicator gives wrong answers — so always use a fresh one!
Scientists wear gloves during experiments to protect their hands from heat, chemicals, and germs.

Why do we wear gloves during experiments?

To protect our hands! They act as a barrier against heat, cuts, or chemicals while we work.
A compound microscope uses two convex lenses! The objective lens near the specimen forms an enlarged image, and the eyepiece magnifies it even further!
When storing the microscope, rotate the nosepiece so the lowest objective is in place, remove the slide, and cover the microscope to protect it from dust.
A microscope magnifies tiny objects hundreds of times — that's how we can see the micro-organisms living in pond water.
A compound microscope uses two convex lenses! The objective lens near the specimen forms an enlarged image, and the eyepiece magnifies it even further!

Carry a compound microscope upright with one hand holding the arm and the other supporting the base. Set it on a stable table. Follow the teacher’s shutdown steps: remove the slide, select the lowest-power objective, switch off the light, and cover for storage in a dry place. Clean lenses only with approved lens paper.
The arm supports the upper part of the microscope and is used to carry it.
Cover the microscope when not in use and store it in a clean, dry place away from corrosive chemical fumes.

Carry a compound microscope upright with one hand holding the arm and the other supporting the base. Set it on a stable table. Follow the teacher’s shutdown steps: remove the slide, select the lowest-power objective, switch off the light, and cover for storage in a dry place. Clean lenses only with approved lens paper.
The nucleus often looks like the darkest round spot inside the cell under the microscope!
Most cells are so tiny your eyes alone can't see them—you need a microscope just to spot a single one.
Every cell has a thin covering called the cell membrane that controls what goes in and out.
The cell membrane is picky — it chooses what to let in, like nutrients, and what to push out, like waste.

Where is DNA found inside a cell?

DNA is found inside the nucleus of the cell.
The nucleus often looks like the darkest round spot inside the cell under the microscope!
Cytoplasm is a jelly-like fluid that fills the cell, and the cell's parts float around inside it.

Start with a teacher-prepared slide at low power, then use fine focus. Compare the visible cell boundary, cytoplasm and nucleus with a labelled reference image. Chloroplasts may be visible in green plant cells. Mitochondria and the thin cell membrane are difficult to distinguish in many ordinary classroom preparations; mark structures learned from references separately from what you actually observe.

Why is mitochondria the cell's powerhouse?

The mitochondria is called the 'powerhouse of the cell' because it produces energy from food.

Start with a teacher-prepared slide at low power, then use fine focus. Compare the visible cell boundary, cytoplasm and nucleus with a labelled reference image. Chloroplasts may be visible in green plant cells. Mitochondria and the thin cell membrane are difficult to distinguish in many ordinary classroom preparations; mark structures learned from references separately from what you actually observe.
Chlorophyll is found tucked inside tiny cell parts called chloroplasts.

Where does photosynthesis happen inside a leaf?

Inside tiny parts of leaf cells called chloroplasts! That's where the chlorophyll is, and where photosynthesis takes place.

Start with a teacher-prepared slide at low power, then use fine focus. Compare the visible cell boundary, cytoplasm and nucleus with a labelled reference image. Chloroplasts may be visible in green plant cells. Mitochondria and the thin cell membrane are difficult to distinguish in many ordinary classroom preparations; mark structures learned from references separately from what you actually observe.
Bacteria multiply by splitting one cell into two.
Bacteria are tiny living things made of just one single cell!
The cell is the smallest unit of life — every living thing is made of one cell or many cells working together!

How many cells are in you?

Your whole body is built from trillions of tiny cells, all working together as a team to keep you alive and healthy.
Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, and mitochondria.

How is a plant cell different from an animal cell?

Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, cell membrane, and cytoplasm—but a plant cell also has a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts for photosynthesis, which animal cells don't have.
A plant cell has a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts that an animal cell doesn't have — that's why the two look so different.

Why do plant cells look boxy?

Animal cells are round or odd-shaped, but plant cells look boxy because of their sturdy cell wall.
A plant cell has a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts that an animal cell doesn't have — that's why the two look so different.

What do plant cells have that animal cells don't?

Three things! Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole — animal cells don't, but they have centrioles that help with cell division instead.

What does the vacuole do in a cell?

The vacuole is a storage sac inside the cell. It holds water, food, and other substances the cell needs.

What does the vacuole do in a plant cell?

Plant cells have a big central vacuole that stores water and helps keep the whole plant firm and standing upright.
During one stage of mitosis, all the chromosomes line up neatly in the middle of the cell.
When a cell divides through mitosis, its two daughter cells each get an exact copy of the same DNA.
When your skin gets wounded, it can heal itself and grow brand-new skin to cover the spot.
From one tiny cell, a baby grows little by little until it weighs a few kilograms before it's born.

Mitosis vs meiosis — what's the difference?

Mitosis makes exact copies of cells for growing and healing. Meiosis makes different sex cells, made for reproduction.
In meiosis, each sex cell gets only half the chromosomes — just one from every pair found in the parent cell.
Half of your chromosomes come from your mother, and the other half come from your father.
During meiosis, chromosomes can swap sections with each other, mixing genes into new combinations and creating more genetic variety.
When egg and sperm unite, the new cell ends up with two of each chromosome — one from the mother and one from the father.
In fertilization, a sex cell from the female (the egg) joins with a sex cell from the male (the sperm) to form a single new cell.
Half of your chromosomes come from your mother, and the other half come from your father.
When egg and sperm unite, the new cell ends up with two of each chromosome — one from the mother and one from the father.
In sexual reproduction, two parents each contribute genes, so their offspring carries a mix of traits from both.
In sexual reproduction, each parent gives half of their genes to their child -- that's why every child has two alleles for each trait.
Tissue culture grows plants in the lab — a tiny plant piece is placed in special nutrient gel to produce many identical copies.

How do bacteria multiply so fast?

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission — one cell splits into two identical cells — letting their numbers grow incredibly quickly.
Similar cells team up to form tissues, and tissues team up to build your organs.
Similar cells group together to form tissues, and tissues build up into organs and body systems.
A population is just one species, like all tilapia in a lake. A community includes many species, like tilapia, snails, and algae together!

Draw and label: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere. In a multicellular organism, similar cells form tissues. A population is one species in an area; a community includes different species. An ecosystem also includes nonliving surroundings. Single-celled organisms do not have tissues or organs.

Draw and label: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere. In a multicellular organism, similar cells form tissues. A population is one species in an area; a community includes different species. An ecosystem also includes nonliving surroundings. Single-celled organisms do not have tissues or organs.

What do arrows from cell to biosphere show in a labelled diagram?

They show that each higher level is made up of the smaller levels right below it!

Why is an energy pyramid pyramid-shaped?

An energy pyramid is wide at the bottom, where producers are, and narrow at the top, because energy is lost at each level of the food chain.

Draw an energy pyramid: rice plants, the producers, at the base; grasshoppers, primary consumers, above; frogs, secondary consumers, higher up. Energy transfers through feeding, but each higher level receives less because organisms use energy and release heat. This example is one feeding path; an omnivore may feed at more than one trophic level.

Draw an energy pyramid: rice plants, the producers, at the base; grasshoppers, primary consumers, above; frogs, secondary consumers, higher up. Energy transfers through feeding, but each higher level receives less because organisms use energy and release heat. This example is one feeding path; an omnivore may feed at more than one trophic level.
Aquatic ecosystems also have energy pyramids, with phytoplankton as producers at the bottom and larger fish as consumers at higher levels.
Energy doesn't get recycled back through the food pyramid -- fresh energy from the sun must keep arriving.
In the ocean, tiny plankton form the huge base of the food pyramid, while sharks at the very top are far fewer in number.
Energy flows in only one direction along a food chain — from plants to the animals that eat them.
At each step of a food chain, a lot of energy is lost as heat — so less and less gets passed on to the next animal.
At each step of a food chain, a lot of energy is lost as heat — so less and less gets passed on to the next animal.

Why are there fewer predators than plants?

It's not just luck — predators are few and plants are many because energy is lost at every level of the food chain.
Small schooling fish eat plankton, and in turn they get eaten by bigger fish like tuna.
Farmers often tie a goat with a rope in one spot so it can munch on grass without wandering off.
A mother whale pushes her newborn to the surface so it can take its first breath.
The gravity of Earth pulls on the Moon, keeping it safely circling around our planet!
The strength of a force is measured in a special unit called the newton!
Did you know? The newton (N) is the special unit we use to measure force!

What happens to the rope in a tug-of-war?

It stays still when both sides pull equally, but moves when one side pulls harder!
A book on a table is in static equilibrium — the table's normal force equals the book's weight, so net force is zero and it stays still!

Do balanced forces always mean an object is standing still?

Nope! Balanced forces can also mean an object is moving straight at a constant speed, like a plane cruising level!

Why do falling objects stop speeding up after a while?

Air resistance grows until it balances gravity! Once they match, the object stops speeding up and falls at a constant speed called terminal velocity.

Ever played tug-of-war?

If one team is stronger, the forces become unbalanced and the rope moves toward them!
When an object keeps the same speed and direction, it has zero acceleration! This means all the forces acting on it are perfectly balanced.
A free-body diagram is a drawing that shows all the forces acting on an object, using arrows that point in the direction and size of each force!
Even when moving at constant velocity, a free-body diagram shows balanced forces with equal and opposite arrows!
When one arrow is longer than the one pointing opposite it, the force is unbalanced and the object accelerates!

How do we draw forces?

Forces are shown using arrows, where the length stands for the strength and the point shows the direction!
When one arrow is longer than the one pointing opposite it, the force is unbalanced and the object accelerates!

How do we draw forces?

Forces are shown using arrows, where the length stands for the strength and the point shows the direction!

For a box resting on a level table, draw a dot with equal-length arrows: weight downward and the table’s support force upward. These forces are balanced. For a horizontal pull of 6 N opposed by 2 N friction, draw the pull arrow three times as long: the net horizontal force is 4 N toward the pull. Label each force and its direction.
Even when moving at constant velocity, a free-body diagram shows balanced forces with equal and opposite arrows!
When one arrow is longer than the one pointing opposite it, the force is unbalanced and the object accelerates!

For a box resting on a level table, draw a dot with equal-length arrows: weight downward and the table’s support force upward. These forces are balanced. For a horizontal pull of 6 N opposed by 2 N friction, draw the pull arrow three times as long: the net horizontal force is 4 N toward the pull. Label each force and its direction.
An unbalanced force is a push or pull that is not canceled out by another force, and it is what changes an object's speed or direction of motion.
A belly-down skydiver hits terminal velocity at 54 meters per second! But diving head-first cuts air resistance, boosting speed past 80 meters per second!

What does the Coriolis effect change about a moving object?

It only changes the direction of a moving object — not how fast it goes!
An unbalanced force is a push or pull that is not canceled out by another force, and it is what changes an object's speed or direction of motion.

What's the difference between distance and displacement?

Distance is the total path length you travel, while displacement is the straight-line gap from start to finish, plus its direction!

Is it possible for your displacement to be zero even if you traveled a really long distance?

Yes! If an object returns to its exact starting point, its displacement is zero, even if the total distance traveled is large.

What's the difference between distance and displacement?

Distance is the total path length you travel, while displacement is the straight-line gap from start to finish, plus its direction!

Is it possible for your displacement to be zero even if you traveled a really long distance?

Yes! If an object returns to its exact starting point, its displacement is zero, even if the total distance traveled is large.

Is it possible for your displacement to be zero even if you traveled a really long distance?

Yes! If an object returns to its exact starting point, its displacement is zero, even if the total distance traveled is large.
Distance can never be negative because it only counts how much ground you covered, and you cannot cover less than zero ground!
Besides speed, the direction of movement also matters to fully describe motion!

What does speed tell us?

Speed tells us exactly how fast an object is moving! Zoom!
Besides speed, the direction of movement also matters to fully describe motion!
Speed only tells how fast something is going, but velocity also includes the direction it is moving!
Speed only tells how fast something is going, but velocity also includes the direction it is moving!

What is the difference between speed and velocity?

Speed tells only how fast something moves, while velocity tells both how fast and in which direction it moves!
Why does a straight line mean constant speed? Because the object adds the same distance every second — equal upward steps mean no curve, just a perfectly straight line!
Distance-time and speed-time graphs are different! In distance-time, height is distance and slope is speed. In speed-time, height is speed, and a flat line means constant speed!
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion, while a flat line means the object is standing still!
On a distance-time graph, a steadily rising line shows a moving object. The steeper the line goes up, the faster its motion!
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion, while a flat line means the object is standing still!
On a distance-time graph, a steadily rising line shows a moving object. The steeper the line goes up, the faster its motion!

For motion east at a uniform velocity of 2 m/s, plot a distance–time graph: (0 s, 0 m), (1 s, 2 m), (2 s, 4 m), (3 s, 6 m). Label time horizontally and distance vertically. A straight rising line shows constant speed. To claim constant velocity too, you must also know the direction stays east; this graph alone does not show direction.
Heat and temperature are different! Temperature measures how hot or cold a thing is, while heat (thermal energy) is the energy transferred from hot to cold.

What is the difference between heat and temperature?

Temperature measures how hot or cold something is! Heat is the energy that flows from a hotter object to a cooler one.

Are temperature and heat the same thing?

Nope! Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy, while heat is the total energy transferred from one object to another.

What is the difference between heat and temperature?

Heat is energy moving from hot to cold objects. Temperature just measures the average motion energy of tiny particles inside!
Use thick oven mitts when touching hot pots! They prevent heat conduction from burning your hands.
Conduction is heat moving through direct touching! Insulation is like a shield that slows this heat down.
Smoke rises from a fire because the hot air around the flame rises, carrying the smoke upward! This is everyday convection we can see.
A thermos has an empty vacuum gap between its walls to block conduction and convection, keeping your drink hot or cold for a long time!
Wear light-colored clothing on sunny days to stay cool! Light colors reflect heat radiation instead of absorbing it.
Dark volcanic rocks around Taal Volcano absorb more solar radiation, making them feel hotter than light-colored sand!
Cooking food well kills the worm eggs and larvae that might be inside it.
Many ice boxes are made of styrofoam! It is full of tiny air pockets that help slow down heat.
Use thick oven mitts when touching hot pots! They prevent heat conduction from burning your hands.
Thick cloth oven mitts act as a thermal insulator, keeping your hands safe from burning on hot pans!
Magma beneath Taal Volcano transfers thermal energy to cooler surrounding rocks through conduction!
In a vacuum gap, there are no particles to carry heat, so it cannot easily spread by conduction or convection!
Warm water is slightly less dense, so it rises right above colder water!
Wind is made when warm air rises up high, and cooler air moves in quickly to take its place!
The Mak-Ban geothermal power plant in Laguna converts underground volcanic heat into electrical energy to power Luzon homes!
Geothermal energy is heat from deep inside the earth! It boils water to make steam that spins a turbine and creates electricity.

Read a reliable science article about a thermoelectric generator. It produces electricity using a temperature difference across suitable materials. Record the source title, the device, its hot and cold sides, and a possible use such as recovering waste heat. Compare claims with evidence; heat is not converted completely into electricity.
Normal faults dip steeply at about 60 degrees! Meanwhile, thrust faults dip gently at 30 degrees or less.

How do rocks move in a normal fault?

The rocks pull apart, and one block drops down! This can make the ground sink and change the shape of the land.
Normal faults dip steeply at about 60 degrees! Meanwhile, thrust faults dip gently at 30 degrees or less.

What happens to rocks in a reverse fault?

The rocks squeeze together, and one block slides up over the other! This can push the seafloor upward during a quake.
The Marikina Valley Fault System in Luzon is a right-lateral strike-slip fault!
The Philippine Fault is a left-lateral strike-slip fault! This means its two sides slide sideways past each other.
Normal faults dip steeply at about 60 degrees! Meanwhile, thrust faults dip gently at 30 degrees or less.
In a strike-slip fault, the fault plane is nearly vertical and the rocks slide past each other horizontally.
The Marikina Valley Fault System in Luzon is a right-lateral strike-slip fault!
When tectonic plates suddenly slip or push against each other, their stored energy is released as a shaking earthquake!
A simple fault model uses two blocks of wood with sandpaper between them! They slide past each other to show how rocks move.
The Marikina Valley Fault System in Luzon is a right-lateral strike-slip fault!
The Valley Fault System running through Marikina is a fracture in Earth's crust that can cause strong earthquakes!
The Richter scale measures the strength or magnitude of an earthquake!
The Richter scale is used to measure the strength or magnitude of an earthquake!
The powerful 1990 Luzon earthquake is a real example of the Philippine Fault moving! It reached magnitude 7.8 and caused heavy damage in Baguio and Cabanatuan.
A high Richter number doesn't always mean severe damage! It only shows the earthquake's strength. Actual damage also depends on depth, distance, and the ground and buildings!
A high Richter number doesn't always mean severe damage! It only shows the earthquake's strength. Actual damage also depends on depth, distance, and the ground and buildings!

What happened during the big Bohol earthquake in 2013?

The magnitude 7.2 quake damaged old churches, changed some Chocolate Hills, and killed over 220 people. It showed we need stronger buildings!
PHIVOLCS has a free tool called FaultFinder! It shows how close your house or school is to an active fault.
PHIVOLCS has a free tool called FaultFinder! It shows exactly how close your house or school is to an active fault.

Why do cities like Manila and Cebu need stronger buildings?

PHIVOLCS seismic zone maps show these areas face high earthquake risk from active faults! This helps us build safer buildings and plan evacuations.

With your teacher, locate your community using PHIVOLCS FaultFinder when available, HazardHunterPH, or an official printed map. Read the legend, scale and date; identify the nearest mapped active fault. Distance to a fault alone does not prove safety: shaking, soil and buildings also matter. Compare findings with your local disaster readiness plan.

What is an epicenter?

It’s the exact spot on the ground right above where an earthquake first starts deep underground!
An earthquake actually starts deep underground at a point called the focus, not at the surface where the epicenter is located!
Magnitude is one number for the whole earthquake's strength at its source, but intensity changes from place to place — stronger near the epicenter!

What is the difference between magnitude and intensity?

Magnitude is computed from the seismograph machine! Intensity is based on what people felt and the damage seen.
Tsunamis don't just come from earthquakes! Underwater landslides and huge underwater volcanic explosions can also create these giant, powerful waves.

Does every earthquake cause a tsunami?

No! It must be strong and shallow, moving the seafloor up or down. If it only slides sideways, usually no tsunami forms.
A simple fault model uses two blocks of wood with sandpaper between them! They slide past each other to show how rocks move.

Draw a cross-section with a sloping fault. Mark the focus where slipping starts underground and the epicenter directly above it. Add two towns: the same earthquake magnitude can produce different intensities because distance, soil and buildings differ. For an offshore fault, draw whether movement displaces the seabed and water above it; not every underwater earthquake generates a tsunami.
During an earthquake, remember to duck, cover under a sturdy table, and hold on tight until the shaking stops!
Philippine schools hold earthquake drills so children can practice what to do and where to go safely during a real earthquake!

What should you do after a strong earthquake?

Calmly go to an open area away from buildings and posts, because aftershocks may still follow!

What should you do when the earthquake shaking finally stops?

Calmly go out to an open area using the evacuation route, because there might still be aftershocks!
Philippine schools hold earthquake drills so children can practice what to do and where to go safely during a real earthquake!
The National Earthquake Drill teaches Filipinos to drop, cover, and hold to stay safe when the West Valley Fault shakes the ground!
When the seafloor shifts, it pushes a huge amount of water upward, and energy spreads outward as waves!
When the seafloor suddenly rises or drops during an earthquake, it pushes the water above it and starts a tsunami!
A powerful tsunami can cross an entire ocean and strike coasts far from where it began!
When a tsunami reaches shallow water near the shore, it slows down. But watch out, because its waves suddenly grow much taller!
When there is a tsunami warning, don't wait! Quickly move to high ground far away from the shore to stay safe.

What should you do during a tsunami warning?

Never go to the shore to watch! Move away and stay on high ground.

Near the coast, strong or long earthquake shaking, an unusual sudden sea rise or fall, or a loud ocean roar can warn of a tsunami. After shaking stops, move promptly along the evacuation route to higher ground or inland; do not wait for an official alert if natural signs occur. Follow PHIVOLCS and local instructions, and return only when authorities say it is safe.
When there is a tsunami warning, don't wait! Quickly move to high ground far away from the shore to stay safe.

What should you do during a tsunami warning?

Never go to the shore to watch! Move away and stay on high ground.

Is it safe to go back to the beach after the first tsunami wave?

No! Do not return to the shore right away because bigger waves can still come.

Is it safe to go back right after the first tsunami wave?

No! A tsunami's danger can last for hours, so it is not yet safe to return after the first wave.

Why is the stratosphere warmer than expected?

Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees!
Earth has seasons because it tilts on its axis as it orbits the Sun!

What really causes Earth's seasons?

Earth's tilted axis changes the angle of sunlight — not its distance from the Sun!
Seasons aren't caused by Earth's distance from the Sun! They happen because Earth's axis is tilted, changing sunlight angles all year.

How does a flashlight act like the Sun?

A straight-down beam is bright, but a slanted beam covers more ground with less light per spot, just like sunlight on Earth!
During the June solstice, the North Pole gets 24 hours of daylight! This is the midnight Sun, so there is no night at all.
In countries far from the equator, the length of daytime changes through the year — long days in summer and short days in winter!

What does a tilted globe and flashlight model show us?

It shows that the lit half of Earth shifts, so some latitudes get more sun time than others.

The amihan is the northeast monsoon wind! It brings cool and dry air to us.
A monsoon is not a storm! It is a wind that blows steadily for many weeks or months, not a big storm passing in one day.
Trade winds are steady winds blowing toward the equator, and when the northern and southern trade winds meet, they form the Intertropical Convergence Zone.
In the Intertropical Convergence Zone, warm air rises continuously, forming tall clouds that often bring heavy rain to places near the equator.
